paragraphs.heading: A flat-topped sea mountain
paragraphs.text: A guyot, also called a tablemount, is a lone volcanic mountain under the sea, a kind of seamount, whose flat top lies more than 200 m below the surface. Those flat summits can be more than 10 km across. They are the ocean's version of tables such as mesas on land. Guyots are most common in the Pacific, but they have been found in every ocean except the Arctic.

paragraphs.heading: Hess and his echo sounder
paragraphs.text: Harry Hammond Hess first recognized guyots in 1945. During World War II he commanded a ship and gathered data with its echo-sounding equipment, which showed that some undersea mountains had flat tops. He named them after the Department of Geosciences building at Princeton. Hess proposed that they had once been volcanic islands whose tops were cut off by waves, even though they now sit deep under the sea. That idea helped support the theory of plate tectonics.

paragraphs.heading: Built up, then planed off
paragraphs.text: Seamounts grow as lava is piped upward in stages from sources inside the mantle, usually hotspots, up to openings in the seafloor. Sooner or later the volcanism always stops, and other processes take over. If an undersea volcano grows close to the surface or breaks through it, waves or growing coral reefs tend to leave it with a flat top.

paragraphs.heading: Slowly sinking
paragraphs.text: All ocean crust and guyots start as hot magma or rock, which cools over time. As the lithosphere carrying the future guyot cools, it grows denser and settles lower into the mantle, a process called isostasy. So the island or shoal slowly sinks over millions of years, and the more time passes, the deeper it goes. Waves and currents wear rock away mostly near the surface, and guyot tops generally lie below that zone.

paragraphs.heading: Reefs that lose the race
paragraphs.text: In the right climate, coral can sometimes grow fast enough to keep up with the sinking, which makes a coral atoll. In the end the reef sinks below the depth where coral can grow, and what is left is a guyot. Guyots carry signs of this path, from a mountain fringed by reef, to an atoll, to a drowned flat-topped peak. The Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain shows every stage, from active volcanoes through reefs and atolls to sunken guyots.

paragraphs.heading: Size and numbers
paragraphs.text: To count as a guyot, a mountain must stand at least 900 m tall, and most have sides sloping at about 20 degrees. The Great Meteor Tablemount in the Northeast Atlantic rises more than 4,000 m and is 110 km wide. On average a guyot covers 3,313 km², far more than a typical seamount at 790 km². There are 283 known guyots, with 119 in the North Pacific alone.
